--- title: "Model Diagnostic" sidebar: start --- The BF class can compute model diagnostics for a given model. Lets consider the following model for a linear regression: $$ Y_i \sim \text{Normal}(\alpha + \beta X_i, \sigma) $$ $$ \alpha \sim \text{Normal}(0, 1) $$ $$ \beta \sim \text{Normal}(0, 1) $$ $$ \sigma \sim \text{Uniform}(0, 50) $$ ::: {.panel-tabset group="language"} ## Python ::: {.cell execution_count=1} ``` {.python .cell-code} from BayesForge import bf import jax.numpy as jnp # setup platform------------------------------------------------ m = bf(platform="cpu") # import data ------------------------------------------------ data_path = m.load.howell1(only_path=True) m.data(data_path, sep=";") m.df = m.df[m.df.age > 18] m.scale(data=["weight"]) # define model ------------------------------------------------ def model(weight, height): a = m.dist.normal(178, 20, name="a") b = m.dist.log_normal(0, 1, name="b") s = m.dist.uniform(0, 50, name="s") m.dist.normal(a + b * weight, s, obs=height, shape=(weight.shape[0],)) # Run sampler ------------------------------------------------ m.fit(model, num_samples=500, num_chains=4) m.summary() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` jax.local_device_count 16 ``` ::: ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ``` 0%| | 0/1500 [00:00
mean sd eti89_lb eti89_ub ess_bulk ess_tail r_hat mcse_mean mcse_sd
a 154.65 0.26 154.24 155.06 2248.81 1641.13 1.0 0.01 0.01
b 5.82 0.28 5.39 6.27 2403.85 1520.09 1.0 0.01 0.01
s 5.14 0.20 4.82 5.47 2089.94 1338.83 1.0 0.00 0.00
``` ::: ::: ## R ```r library(BayesForge) # setup platform------------------------------------------------ m <- importBF(platform = "cpu") # import data ------------------------------------------------ data_path <- m$load$howell1(only_path = TRUE) m$data(data_path, sep = ";") m$df <- m$df[m$df$age > 18, ] m$scale(list("weight")) m$data_to_model(list("weight", "height")) # define model ------------------------------------------------ model <- function(weight, height) { a <- bf.dist.normal(178, 20, name = "a") b <- bf.dist.log_normal(0, 1, name = "b") s <- bf.dist.uniform(0, 50, name = "s") bf.dist.normal(a + b * weight, s, obs = height, name = "height") } # Run sampler ------------------------------------------------ m$fit(model, num_samples = 500, num_chains = 4) m$summary() ``` ## Julia ```julia using PyBayesForge # setup platform------------------------------------------------ m = importBF(platform = "cpu") # import data ------------------------------------------------ data_path = m.load.howell1(only_path = true) m.data(data_path, sep = ";") m.df = m.df[m.df.age > 18] m.scale(["weight"]) # define model ------------------------------------------------ @BF function model(weight, height) a = m.dist.normal(178, 20, name = "a") b = m.dist.log_normal(0, 1, name = "b") s = m.dist.uniform(0, 50, name = "s") m.dist.normal(a + b * weight, s, obs = height) end # Run sampler ------------------------------------------------ m.fit(model, num_samples = 500, num_chains = 4) m.summary() ``` ::: # List of all available diagnostics For additional documentation check the [diagnostics API reference](../reference/diag.qmd) Every plot takes `x_label=` and `y_label=` to replace the axis titles (`title=` for the plot title). A string sets the title of every panel; a list sets one per panel, in order (`None` keeps a panel's own title), for example `m.diag.posterior(x_label=["intercept", "slope", "sigma"])`. ## Predictions from model based on specific data value By default (`posterior=True`, `samples=None`), `m.sample(...)` evaluates the predictive distribution across all posterior MCMC draws (here $500 \times 4 = 2000$ draws). To obtain a single predicted value instead of the full posterior predictive vector, you can draw a single sample (`samples=1`), take the posterior predictive mean, or evaluate at fixed parameter values (`posterior=...`): ::: {.panel-tabset group="language"} ## Python ::: {.cell execution_count=2} ``` {.python .cell-code} m.sample() # Predictions from model based on data in data_on_model pred = m.sample(data=dict(weight=jnp.array([0.4])), remove_obs=False) # Full posterior predictive (2000 draws) # 1. Single random predictive draw from the posterior m.sample(data=dict(weight=jnp.array([0.4])), remove_obs=False, samples=1) # 2. Posterior predictive mean across all 2000 draws jnp.mean(pred["height"]) # 3. Single draw at fixed parameter values m.sample( data=dict(weight=jnp.array([0.4])), posterior=dict(a=154.6, b=5.8, s=5.1), remove_obs=False, ) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=31} ``` {'height': Array([[157.4768534]], dtype=float64)} ``` ::: ::: ## R ```r m$sample() # Predictions from model based on data in data_on_model pred <- m$sample(data = list(weight = jnp$array(c(0.4))), remove_obs = FALSE) # Full posterior predictive (2000 draws) # 1. Single random predictive draw from the posterior m$sample(data = list(weight = jnp$array(c(0.4))), remove_obs = FALSE, samples = 1L) # 2. Posterior predictive mean across all 2000 draws jnp$mean(pred$height) # 3. Single draw at fixed parameter values m$sample( data = list(weight = jnp$array(c(0.4))), posterior = list(a = 154.6, b = 5.8, s = 5.1), remove_obs = FALSE ) ``` ## Julia ```julia m.sample() # Predictions from model based on data in data_on_model pred = m.sample(data = pydict(weight = jnp.array([0.4])), remove_obs = false) # Full posterior predictive (2000 draws) # 1. Single random predictive draw from the posterior m.sample(data = pydict(weight = jnp.array([0.4])), remove_obs = false, samples = 1) # 2. Posterior predictive mean across all 2000 draws jnp.mean(pred["height"]) # 3. Single draw at fixed parameter values m.sample( data = pydict(weight = jnp.array([0.4])), posterior = pydict(a = 154.6, b = 5.8, s = 5.1), remove_obs = false ) ``` ::: ## Forest plot of estimated values ::: {.panel-tabset group="language"} ## Python ::: {.cell execution_count=10} ``` {.python .cell-code} m.diag.plot_ess() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ``` Unable to display output for mime type(s): text/html ``` ::: ::: ## R ```r m$diag$plot_ess() ``` ## Julia ```julia @pyplot m.diag.plot_ess() ``` ::: See [`m.diag.plot_ess`](../reference/diag.qmd#plot_ess) for further information regarding the list of arguments. ## HMC diagnostics: divergences and energy Check this plot first: if the sampler failed, the other diagnostics are not meaningful. - **Top row, one panel per chain:** the distribution of the energy E around its mean (blue, *marginal energy*) and of its change between two successive iterations, ΔE (orange, *energy transition*). When the two histograms have about the same width, the sampler can cross the whole posterior from one iteration to the next. When ΔE is much narrower than E, it explores the tails badly (typical of a hierarchical "funnel"). The panel title gives E-BFMI = Σ ΔE² / Σ (E − Ē)²; values below 0.3 are flagged with ⚠. - **Bottom row:** the number of divergent transitions per chain (ideal: 0). A divergence means that the integrator failed in a region of strong curvature, which is then under-explored. With a few divergences, raise `target_accept` (0.95–0.99); with many, reparametrise (for example a non-centred random effect). ::: {.panel-tabset group="language"} ## Python ::: {.cell execution_count=11} ``` {.python .cell-code} m.diag.divergence_energy() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ``` Unable to display output for mime type(s): text/html ``` ::: ::: ## Regression plot Observed data plus n smooth posterior regression lines E[y | x, theta] and their posterior mean, overlaid against a predictor variable. ::: {.panel-tabset group="language"} ## Python ::: {.cell execution_count=23} ``` {.python .cell-code} m.diag.plot_regression("weight", n = 20) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ``` Unable to display output for mime type(s): text/html ``` ::: ::: ## R ```r m$diag$plot_regression("weight", n = 20L) ``` ## Julia ```julia @pyplot m.diag.plot_regression("weight", n = 20) ``` ::: See [`m.diag.plot_regression`](../reference/diag.qmd#plot_regression) for further information regarding the list of arguments. ## Sensitivity ### Prior sensitivity Overlays the posteriors from models fitted with different priors to assess how much the conclusions change when the priors vary. ::: {.panel-tabset group="language"} ## Python ::: {.cell execution_count=24} ``` {.python .cell-code} # Refit the same model with a tighter prior on b posteriors_weak = m.posteriors def model_strong(weight, height): a = m.dist.normal(178, 20, name="a") b = m.dist.log_normal(0, 0.1, name="b") s = m.dist.uniform(0, 50, name="s") m.dist.normal(a + b * weight, s, obs=height, shape=(weight.shape[0],)) m.fit(model_strong, num_samples=500, num_chains=4) m.diag.prior_sensitivity([posteriors_weak, m.posteriors], labels=["weak prior", "strong prior"]) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ``` 0%| | 0/1500 [00:00 0.7 (red line, red points) | very influential observation; LOO is unreliable for it | A few red points are often outliers or data errors (hover to see their index and value). Many red points mean the model is misspecified or too flexible (for example one parameter per observation); try a robust likelihood (Student-t) or a more structured model. When some k exceed 0.7, model comparison with `m.diag.loo()` / `compare` is not reliable. ::: {.panel-tabset group="language"} ## Python ::: {.cell execution_count=25} ``` {.python .cell-code} m.diag.influence() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ``` Unable to display output for mime type(s): text/html ``` ::: ::: ## R ```r m$diag$influence() ``` ## Julia ```julia @pyplot m.diag.influence() ``` ::: See [`m.diag.influence`](../reference/diag.qmd#influence) for further information regarding the list of arguments. ### Calibration For several interval levels (50%, 60%, ..., 99%), the share of observed values that actually fall inside the predictive interval of that level (y axis) against the level itself (x axis); the dashed diagonal is perfect calibration. Points below the diagonal (the "90%" interval contains only, say, 70% of the data) mean the model is over-confident, which is the most serious case; points above it mean the model is too cautious. These intervals are not leave-one-out, so a slight over-coverage is expected. ::: {.panel-tabset group="language"} ## Python ::: {.cell execution_count=26} ``` {.python .cell-code} m.diag.calibration() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` ⚠️This function is still in development.
